title: Sonatine (1993): the ubermensch and a modern-day appropriation of bushido

commenti.body: I didn't understand his concept of the ubermensch as a return to some ancient master morality. His ubermensch is beyond good and evil, who doesn't let any morality outside of themselves dictate their behavior. They completely create their own values whatever they might be.

As sort of an interesting aside, Nietzsche did not present the Übermensch as something we should all achieve. In fact, anyone reading his books are supposed to be aware of the fact that they are merely the start of a journey towards the future, and at the same time a necessary end to what came before.

But his writing is often taken as a sort of "guide" to becoming this heralded kind of figure. His writing makes it likely to happen, unless one spends a lot of time with all his texts (and, we might add, in a professional capacity). It's an obvious theme to hook onto, and he does to some extent invite the reader into that theme - but, critically, _nobody_ becomes the Übermensch. They are still merely human.

It's one of the tricky things in Nietzsche.
Thanks! I've only read Zarathustra (years ago), and am now immersing myself in Morality. So I'm just operating from my reading and of course, general understanding.

Your understanding of Nietzsche is way off here. The Ubermensch’s moral system is a not a return to the master morality system. It is a creative transcendence of both master and slave morality. The “popular” conception of the Ubermensch is what you’ve reiterated here, which is a kind of Machiavellian amoral antihero.
